title: Opening to Joy
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan tells of a 2016 trip to Rinso-in in Japan, where Hoitsu, son of Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, recalls a father who threw him in the pond for forgetting his schoolwork, then ends with the words "Practice with joy." Seiu brings in James Baraz's picture of the brain as Teflon for good experiences and Velcro for bad, and asks the room to call out what brings them joy. The center is mudita, sympathetic joy, one of the four Brahmaviharas, along with Seiu's memories of measuring up against others and a guided practice that moves from oneself to a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person, and all beings. The closing names Dogen's three minds and Kate, who shows joy in how she appreciates others' good fortune.

Well, good morning.

Hi, Elizabeth.
We have one Zoom person.
The invitation was to talk on the topic of opening to joy.
In 2016, I had the good fortune of traveling to Japan.
The trip was led by two great practitioners and dharma friends, Myoshin Kate McCandless and Shinman Michael Newton, the guiding teachers at Mountain Rain in Vancouver.
We're happy to have two of our practitioners from Dharma Rain here today, and I think we'll see another one later, so welcome.

Kate and Michael met as grad students in Asian studies while living in Kyoto, so they were very familiar with both the language and the area, and they led two trips for practitioners prior to our trip.
Their fluency in the language and their familiarity with Soto practice and our lineage through Shinryo Suzuki Roshi allowed us a five-day stay at Rinso-in, the home temple.
That home temple was also visited in April by our group from Red Cedar.
Suzuki Roshi's son Hoitsu, also known as Hojo-san, was in residence along with his wife, their son, and his family, and we were able to have a short sesshin there.
On the last day, Hoitsu gave us a Dharma talk, mostly translated by Michael.
He suggested that we might want to know what it was like to grow up with Suzuki Roshi for a father.

In addition to the good things, he told us the unvarnished version, and it included Suzuki Roshi's realization that they were quite a bit alike, and he didn't want his son to be burdened by his own shortcomings.
Forgetfulness was one of the things, and it must have been excruciating for a father to see a son walking into some of the habits that had been problematic for him.
So one day, Hoitsu was leaving for school, and it was noticed that he'd forgotten his books and his schoolwork, so his dad threw him into the pond.
Anger was an issue.

At a later time, a troubled townsperson, who had shown violent tendencies and mental health issues, was allowed to keep returning to the temple out of compassion and kindness, and one day that person attacked and killed Suzuki Roshi's mother.
I'm sorry, Suzuki Roshi's wife, Hoitsu's mother.

Later, when Suzuki Roshi had gone to San Francisco, his earnings at the local temple were bare bones, just enough to survive in the city, and he was unable to send money back to Japan for Hoitsu to attend college as had been planned.
It was through the generosity of a grandmother that he was finally able to attend.
We listened, rapt, as we envisioned this crazy life of tears, which is a part of the title of Norman's reflections on his trip to Japan and his relationship with Hoitsu.
In closing, his statement was this, and he said it in English, and so I must tell you: "Practice with joy."
I've never forgotten that, and the friends I traveled with didn't forget it either.

Stress increases this tendency, and also confirmation bias, if you are familiar with that term: it's a tendency to interpret new evidence as confirmation of one's existing beliefs or theories.
So our brain picks up everything we have in that belief system and through repetition shapes the lens that we look through.
Are we condemned?
I should tell you the full title of Norman's aforementioned book, which was in fact a direct quote from a Dharma talk that he heard from Hoitsu.
The full title is Escape This Crazy Life of Tears.
After all, he is a Buddhist teacher.
Where would he derive wisdom?
We might look to the Four Noble Truths, one of the foundations of our practice.
One, there is suffering.
Two, the cause is perpetuation through repetition of the same actions.
Three, there is a way out.
And four is the Eightfold Path.

Yeah, there is suffering.
Nobody here has been immune to that.

And yet, his gentle message was always love, peace.
So how do you do that when you have seen a crazy life of tears?

How can we cultivate happiness or the experience of joy?

What brings you joy?
How does it feel?

Exaltation, perhaps.
What about the gladness connected to a moment of generosity?

I'm sorry, six times a day for a total of 90 seconds.

It's an attitude.
It's an intention.
It's a way of being.

If there was one calm person on the raft, it had a better chance of surviving.
We can actually be that person if we choose.

This brings to mind one of the ancient Buddhist teachings, the Brahma Viharas.
They're also known as the Four Abodes.

You might call this a teenage secular awakening.
He was climbing St.
Helens with Boy Scouts, which for him, not too many years later, developed into a formal Zen Bodhisattva vow to bring others across before himself.

The surprises along the way.
A really interesting plant in bloom.
The smell of the trees.
Gazing at water.
I referenced also in that same talk the idea of the blue mind, the concept that originated with the late marine biologist Wallace J.
Nichols.
He is describing the phenomenon that looking at water will engender a mildly meditative state.

It's inspired by water, and it takes advantage of the neurological connections formed over millennia that are still being discovered via newer technology, including EEG and MRI, where we can pick up changes in the brain based on meditation, based on engendering of the positive.

You may be deficient in vitamin D, or in B12.
You may find joy in playing an instrument, dancing, as was said before, cooking, arranging flowers, riding a bike, looking at paintings, painting, doing a sculpture.
And depending on your life circumstances, you may find inspiration in the presence or the absence of other people.
How might we live out that Bodhisattva vow?
Dogen wrote that someone working to benefit others, as I said, should maintain three minds, also known as magnanimous mind, parental mind, and joyful mind.
I'd like to say that one person I have really learned from by her demonstration of joy is Kate.
She brings joy.
She appreciates the good fortune of others, no matter what may be arising for her personally.
She wishes well-being for the world.
May we all find joy.
May we all appreciate the joy of others.
How can we not if, in fact, we are inter-being, connected by one body, one Buddha?
Thank you for listening.
